title: Optimising model cost before proving the task works—or ignoring economics once it does
summary: Establish capability inside a budget, then optimise the complete cost of successful delivery.
diagnosis: A cheap model that fails does not prove a use case is infeasible, and an expensive configuration that works does not prove it is economical. Separate the feasibility question from the operating-cost question without postponing all financial discipline. Test a sufficiently capable baseline, identify why it succeeds or fails, and then compare cheaper or simpler configurations against the same quality boundary.
diagnostic_questions: Is the initial configuration capable enough to test the idea, or is cost minimisation masking feasibility?
Which costs sit outside model tokens: retrieval, integrations, retries, human review and support?
Can spending grow through loops, concurrent jobs or unexpected demand even if each request looks cheap?
proposed_actions: Allocate a bounded feasibility budget and define acceptable completion before comparing model configurations.
Benchmark complete alternatives on representative work; include routing, deterministic components and escalation rather than only model substitution.
Install per-task and aggregate spending limits, then revisit economics when volume, quality, prices or review requirements change.
working_artifact: Unit-economics worksheet specification: eligible task; acceptance rule; model/tool costs; retries; human review minutes; support allocation; fixed implementation cost; volume assumptions; sensitivity ranges; stopping limits.
measures: Quality-adjusted cost per accepted task, with the success rate and review burden visible alongside the average.
Budget consumption by experiment, workflow and team, including failed and abandoned attempts.
Sensitivity of the business case to volume, difficult-case frequency, review time and provider changes.
tradeoff: The largest model is not a mandatory starting point, and the cheapest is not a mandatory destination. Some exploration has learning value before a full return estimate is possible, but the organisation should still know the maximum exposure it has authorised.
illustrative_case: Illustrative application: a cheaper model lowers request cost but doubles correction time. A more capable model or a hybrid may be less expensive per accepted result. The reverse may be true once the workflow is better specified.
